coverageNote: Enumerated from disk: 7 unit directories containing an *-index.md (the domain root plus 20.01-20.06) and 41 .md files total, exactly matching the expected 7 units / 41 files. Every file was read in full via the sandbox and passed through the 3a implementer-simulation, 3b rubric scoring and 3c devil's-advocate cycle. The domain-root unit comprises fanbase-direct-to-fan-index.md, fanbase-direct-to-fan-cx.md and the domain-level leaf feature 20.07-fan-demand-show-requests.md. Rubric dimensions 2 (Persona Specificity), 4 (Constraint Explicitness) and 6 (Competitive Positioning) are marked N/A for every unit: personas are referenced from meta/personas.md and never redefined here (the correct cross-reference pattern), constraints live in meta/constraints.md, and competitive positioning belongs to meta/competitive-landscape.md. Dimensions 1, 3, 5, 7 and 8 are applicable to all 7 units, giving 5 checkpoints per unit. Devil's-advocate pass dropped 4 candidate findings that did not survive: (a) the domain CX status line counting '13 High, 1 Medium' against a table showing 12 High / 2 Medium - a pure metadata tally error that changes nothing about what is built; (b) the domain index Children table showing all children as [SURFACE] while their files are [BREADTH]/[DEEP]/[PARTIAL] - line 34 explicitly frames that column as the Step-3 breadth snapshot, a defensible historical record; (c) 20.05.03's Role Lens granting the Producer 'Reports (as split payee)' against D-03 'splits do not apply' - the Role Lens text is explicitly conditional on the unresolved Q-01 and is therefore consistent; (d) 20.01.04's edge-case [PENDING] on stale-consent import - it cross-references 20.01.02 Q-02, which is properly tracked with owner and deferral target.

units.detail: Dim 1 OK. Dim 3 FAIL (blocking vault-lapse contradiction in fanbase-direct-to-fan-cx.md CX-14). Dim 5 OK. Dim 7 OK - every Q-01..Q-10 on the index and Q-01..Q-05 on 20.07 carries an owner and a deferral target or an explicit resolution. Dim 8 WARN (Role Matrix rollup contradicts 20.05.06's Operator grant).

Dim 3 WARN - three behaviour-level imprecisions (identity-based marketing gate stated then denied; the `service` consent purpose has no send-time resolution; the Highlights frequency cap is described both per-email and per-send). Dims 1, 5, 7, 8 OK: quantified thresholds throughout (24-month staleness, 80 km / 10-500 km radius, 7-day undo, RFC 8058), and every open question carries owner + deferral target.

Dim 3 WARN (over-promise: 'blocked at grant time' vs user-facing copy offering a proceed-with-disclosure path). Dim 7 WARN (stale bare [PENDING] markers in 20.02.02 edge cases, no owner and no deferral target, contradicted by that file's own D-01/D-04). Dims 1, 5, 8 OK.

Dim 3 WARN (object-derived urgent operational sends are routed to CX-M07 transactional transport by 20.03.02 DT-04 and simultaneously given a priority lane inside broadcast throttling by 20.03.03 D-06). Dims 1, 5, 7, 8 OK - unusually strong: every deferral names an owner and a stage, and the sub-domain's own D-02 non-overridable-throttle rule is consistently applied across all four leaves.

Dim 3 WARN (payout-plan version bound at 'payment settlement' in 20.04.03 vs 'payment authorization' in 20.04.04; 10% rolling reserve described both per-disbursement and per-accrual, leaving the 90-day clock start undefined). Dim 7 WARN (20.04-...-cx.md CX-01 Q5 still marked [PENDING] and 'the unsolved case' after 20.04.03 D-06 explicitly resolves it by name). Dims 1, 5, 8 OK - this is the most quantitatively specified sub-domain in the tree.

All applicable dimensions pass. Every hard question (advance tranche, milestone verification, insolvency, keep-vs-lose on lapse, all-or-nothing) is explicitly open with an [OWNER] tag and a named stage, and the files are candid about what they cannot resolve rather than inventing an answer. No forced inventions found.

Dim 3 WARN (the surviving-on-lapse set is 'items opened while entitled' in 20.05.02 but 'items released while the fan was paying' in 20.06.03 - two different sets). Dim 5 WARN (20.06.02 D-05 mandates an alerting SLO with no target value and no deferral routing it anywhere). Dims 1, 7, 8 OK; the radius conflict between 20.06.02 and 20.01.03 is explicitly recorded and tracked as 20.06.02 Q-05 [OWNER] and is therefore not a finding.

findings.claim: The domain cross-cut file states that membership-gated vault items lock the instant a membership lapses and must fail closed to locked, while both leaf files that own the behaviour state the opposite - that items the fan already had while paying stay accessible and only future items lock. Neither statement carries a marker, and the two cannot both hold.
findings.evidence: fanbase-direct-to-fan-cx.md:25 - "**The vault-lapse race.** Membership-gated vault items ([20.05.02](...)) **lock the instant a membership lapses**, and that lock is *felt in the fan's library*"; fanbase-direct-to-fan-cx.md:356 - "Lapse (billing event, CX-M24) -> membership state change (20.05.01) -> vault entitlement re-evaluated (20.05.02) -> library row locks (20.06.03). Must be atomic-enough that the library never shows a stale *unlocked* state after a lapse - fail-closed to locked on ambiguity."; fanbase-direct-to-fan-cx.md:357 - "Distinguish member-*gated* vault content (re-locks) from *purchased* content (never re-locks)". Against: 20.05-memberships-patronage-campaigns/20.05.02-exclusive-content-vault.md:73 - "until ratified, the safe default is no retroactive removal (matches D-05); items opened while entitled stay accessible"; 20.06-fan-experience-discovery/20.06.03-fan-library-collection.md:120 - "on lapse, per [20.05.02](...) DT-02's leaning, items **released while the fan was paying stay accessible** and future items lock." CX-14 section 5 defers only "whether *previously downloaded* copies survive" to 20.05.02 Q-01, so its unqualified re-lock claim about in-vault access is not covered by that deferral.
findings.forcedInvention: An implementer must invent whether a lapsed member retains in-product access to vault items they held while paying, or loses all member-gated items at the lapse instant.
findings.failure_scenario: A fan holds a GBP 10/month tier for 14 months, opens 30 vault demos, then lets the membership lapse. An implementer following fanbase-direct-to-fan-cx.md CX-14 builds an atomic fail-closed re-lock: all 30 items grey out at the lapse instant. An implementer following 20.05.02 and 20.06.03 builds the opposite: those 30 stay playable and only items posted after the lapse lock. The two builds are mutually exclusive, and 20.05.01's edge-case row explicitly warns the wrong choice is the one that generates chargebacks ("a fan who loses a year of demos feels robbed").

findings.claim: The domain-level Role Matrix gives the Operator no access at all across sub-domain 20.05, but the 20.05 sub-domain index and the 20.05.06 feature file both grant the Operator Config access on Virtual Fan Events. The rollup row and the child grant state different current-state answers.
findings.evidence: fanbase-direct-to-fan-index.md:95 - "| 20.05 Memberships, Patronage & Campaigns | \u2705 Full | \ud83d\udcca Reports (payee) | \u274c None \u2014 see Q-04 | \ud83d\udc41\ufe0f Read-only (joins, backs, attends) |". Against: 20.05-memberships-patronage-campaigns/20.05-memberships-patronage-campaigns-index.md:47 - "| 20.05.06 Virtual Fan Events | \u2705 Full | \u274c None | \u2699\ufe0f Config \u2014 see Q-04 | \ud83d\udc41\ufe0f Read-only (attends) |"; 20.05-memberships-patronage-campaigns/20.05.06-virtual-fan-events.md:25 - "| Operator | Config | Index Q-04 \u2014 currently narrow. **A grassroots venue streaming its own shows to a supporter scheme is a real, underserved product**". The cited Q-04 asks only whether an Operator can run *memberships*; whether an Operator can run *events* is a separate tracked question (20.05.06 Q-03), so the deferral does not reconcile the two matrix cells.
findings.forcedInvention: An implementer must invent whether the Operator persona gets any interface at all on Virtual Fan Events.
findings.failure_scenario: A developer scoping Operator navigation reads the domain Role Matrix, sees 20.05 = None, and ships no venue-side event surface. A developer scoping the 20.05.06 slice reads that file's Role Lens, sees Config, and ships an Operator event-scheduling screen. Two slices of the same release disagree on whether a venue can schedule a livestream, and QA has no authoritative row to test against.

findings.claim: 20.01.01 states in one edge-case row that marketing is disabled on a guest-purchase record until a stronger identity key confirms, and in another row states categorically that key strength gates resolution 'and nothing beyond that' and that this node holds no second identity-based marketing gate. The row-80 reconciliation covers only records with no usable address, not the row-66 case where a payment email was supplied.
findings.evidence: 20.01-fan-graph-owned-audience/20.01.01-unified-fan-record.md:66 - "Anonymous/guest purchase, no account | Record created keyed on payment-instrument fingerprint (+ payment email if provided). Weaker; resolves later if that human ever logs in with the same address/instrument. | Artist sees the record marked **unverified-identity**; marketing disabled until a stronger key confirms." Against: 20.01-fan-graph-owned-audience/20.01.01-unified-fan-record.md:80 - "Key strength gates **resolution**, not marketing - it decides whether an observation auto-merges or only proposes a merge (D-02), and nothing beyond that. This node does not hold a second, identity-based marketing gate: contactability is governed entirely by [20.01.02](...)" and, in the same row, "Where the weakest key is a payment fingerprint or a processor-hidden email the record has no marketing-capable address at all, so it is not contactable as a matter of fact rather than of policy".
findings.forcedInvention: An implementer must invent whether a guest-purchase record carrying a usable payment email is marketable once a marketing consent event exists, or is blocked on identity strength regardless of consent.
findings.failure_scenario: A fan checks out as a guest, supplies a real payment email and ticks the marketing opt-in box. Following row 66 the implementer suppresses that fan from every campaign until they log in with a stronger key, so the artist's segment silently omits a lawfully consented buyer. Following row 80 the implementer includes them on the strength of the consent event alone. The two builds produce different contactable counts from identical data, and 20.02.01 D-04 makes that count artist-visible.

findings.claim: The consent model defines three orthogonal purposes - marketing, transactional and service - and states normatively that a marketing grant does not authorise service messages, but no file in the domain defines how a `service` purpose resolves at send time. The send-time resolution rule has only two branches and the campaign purpose-type enum has no `service` member.
findings.evidence: 20.01-fan-graph-owned-audience/20.01.02-consent-legal-basis.md:38-39 - "**which purpose** it authorises (marketing, transactional, or service)"; same file, DT-04 at line 115 - "A `marketing` grant does not imply a right to send `service` messages". Against: 20.01-fan-graph-owned-audience/20.01.03-fan-preference-centre.md:57-62 - "each campaign carries a purpose-type - `transactional`, `general`, `release`, or `live-event-geo` ... Resolution per fan, in order: (1) `transactional` always passes, untouched by any tier or channel mute ...; (2) marketing passes only if the entity is not globally opted out, **and** ... A campaign left **untagged defaults to `general`**". No file maps `service` to a campaign purpose-type, and 20.01.02's Q-03 asks only "Where exactly is the line between `transactional` and `marketing`?" - `service` is not covered by any tracked question in the domain.
findings.forcedInvention: An implementer must invent whether service messages exist as a sendable class, whether they pass the global opt-out and per-channel mutes, and whether they count against a frequency tier's cap.
findings.failure_scenario: The platform needs to send an account-security or membership-state notice classified as `service`. One implementer treats service like transactional (always passes, ignores tiers), so a fan on the per-entity Off tier receives it. Another treats it as marketing (gated by global opt-out and the tier cap), so the same fan receives nothing. 20.01.02 DT-04 says both readings are wrong - the purposes are orthogonal, not nested - but supplies no third rule.

findings.claim: The Highlights frequency tier is defined in one column as a cap of one marketing email per calendar month and in the adjacent column of the same row as dropping the second-plus marketing send, while the tier is separately declared orthogonal to the per-channel toggles. Whether the cap is email-only or covers every channel is not stated.
findings.evidence: 20.01-fan-graph-owned-audience/20.01.03-fan-preference-centre.md:44 - "Frequency is a **per-(fan, entity)** setting, orthogonal to the per-channel toggles and to the global opt-out."; same file line 50 - "| **Highlights** | At most **1 marketing email per calendar month** from this entity | The 2nd+ marketing send in a month is **dropped, not queued** | \"Monthly digest\". Cap is per-entity, not global. |"; D-05 at line 163 restates it as "Highlights (\u22641 email/month)". 20.03-broadcast-fan-messaging/20.03.03-send-scheduling-throttling.md:61 inherits the same wording - "A fan on **Highlights** admits at most one marketing email per calendar month from this entity and the second is **dropped, not queued**" - without resolving whether SMS or push consume the same allowance.
findings.forcedInvention: An implementer must invent whether an SMS or push campaign consumes a Highlights-tier fan's monthly allowance, or whether each channel carries its own independent monthly cap.
findings.failure_scenario: A fan sets an artist to Highlights and keeps both email and SMS enabled. The artist sends a release email on the 3rd and a tour SMS on the 20th. Reading the cap as per-send, the SMS is dropped and the artist's report shows a suppression. Reading it as per-email, the SMS goes out and the fan who explicitly asked for 'one thing a month' receives two - the exact over-sending the tier exists to prevent, and on the channel with TCPA exposure (20.03.02 line 37).

findings.claim: 20.02.03 D-03 states that an over-promised entitlement is blocked at grant time, while the edge-case row that D-03 cites specifies user-facing copy offering the artist a second path - saying plainly that it is first-come - which implies the grant proceeds. Whether the first-come label is an escape hatch from the block is not stated.
findings.evidence: 20.02-segmentation-superfan-intelligence/20.02.03-perk-entitlements-presale-eligibility.md:96 - "| D-03 | Over-promise is blocked at grant time | See DT-02. Disappointing your best fans is the worst outcome this feature can produce, and it is entirely preventable. |". Against the same file line 54 - "Presale allocation smaller than the eligible set | **The most common real failure.** 1,203 eligible, 300 tickets. ... Must be caught at grant time, not at on-sale. | \"You're promising 1,203 fans access to 300 tickets. Narrow the audience, or say plainly that it's first-come.\"" DT-02 at line 76 adds only that the check "must be blunt rather than a warning nobody reads", which does not distinguish a hard refusal from a forced relabel.
findings.forcedInvention: An implementer must invent whether an artist can complete an over-subscribed grant by labelling it first-come, or whether the grant is refused outright until the audience is narrowed.
findings.failure_scenario: An artist grants a 48-hour presale to a 1,203-fan segment against a 300-ticket allocation. A hard-block implementation refuses the grant, and the artist - who genuinely wants a first-come presale, a normal industry practice - cannot run one at all. A relabel implementation lets it through with a first-come badge, which D-03 reads as exactly the over-promise it forbids. The two ship different, incompatible presale products.

findings.claim: Two edge-case rows in 20.02.02 carry a bare [PENDING] with no owner and no deferral target, and both mark as unresolved a question that the same file's Decisions table already answers. The tracking is malformed and stale in the same place.
findings.evidence: 20.02-segmentation-superfan-intelligence/20.02.02-superfan-score.md:72 - "New artist, no purchase/scan history | Score degrades to open/click ... | `[PENDING]` - the honest answer may be to withhold scoring until there is signal, rather than show a confident number built on nothing." and line 73 - "Wealthy fan vs devoted broke fan | Spend-weighted scoring ranks a rich casual above a devoted teenager ... See DT-01. | `[PENDING]`". Both are already decided in the same file: line 117 - "| D-04 | Withhold the score rather than show a low-confidence one | Cold-start (DT-02). An artist who trusts a fabricated rank makes worse decisions than one who knows they lack data. |"; line 114 - "| D-01 | Attendance (scans) outweighs spend | See DT-01 and DT-04. |"; and the States table at line 85 specifies the UI - "Empty | Insufficient signal | An explicit \"not enough signal yet\" - not a zero, not a low band."
findings.forcedInvention: None - the answers exist in the same file; the defect is that two rows assert an open question with no owner and no deferral target against decisions that already close them.
findings.failure_scenario: An implementer building the cold-start UI reads the edge-case table first (the conventional place to look for it), finds [PENDING] with no owner and no stage to chase, and either blocks the slice awaiting a ruling that was already made or invents a low-confidence band display - directly contradicting D-04 and the specified Empty state.

findings.claim: 20.03.02 states categorically that an urgent operational change such as a cancelled show is a transactional message belonging to CX-M07's transport rather than to broadcast, while 20.03.03 - a child of the broadcast sub-domain - gives exactly those object events a priority lane inside broadcast's own scheduling and throttling machinery. The two files place the same message class in two different machines with different consent gates and different channel-selection rules.
findings.evidence: 20.03-broadcast-fan-messaging/20.03.02-channel-routing-bulk-delivery.md:87 (DT-04) - "An urgent operational change (\"doors moved\", \"show cancelled\") is a **transactional** message tied to a purchase/relationship, which belongs to CX-M07's transport, where consent is implied by the relationship and channel is chosen by urgency. This feature is **marketing broadcast** ... So there is no legitimate \"artist override\" *here*: if it is urgent enough to override preference, it is not a marketing broadcast." Against: 20.03-broadcast-fan-messaging/20.03.03-send-scheduling-throttling.md:105 - "| D-06 | Urgency is object-derived, never artist-asserted; urgent sends bypass the warm-up ramp but not quiet hours or the circuit-breaker | ... a platform-recognised cancelled/changed show (domain 17) is urgent by nature" and the same file line 56 - "Such a send takes a priority lane that bypasses the warm-up ramp but still respects statutory quiet hours and the hard deliverability circuit-breaker".
findings.forcedInvention: An implementer must invent which machine dispatches a show-cancellation notice - CX-M07 transactional transport with urgency-chosen channel, or 20.03 broadcast with the fan's channel preference sovereign under 20.03.02 D-06.
findings.failure_scenario: A show is cancelled four hours before doors. Routed through CX-M07 the platform picks the channel by urgency and SMSes every ticket holder including those who muted SMS for marketing. Routed through 20.03.03's priority lane, 20.03.02 D-06 makes the fan's channel choice sovereign, so a fan who muted SMS gets only an email they will not read before travelling to the venue. The same event produces materially different fan outcomes depending on which file the implementer followed.

findings.claim: The two files that own the buy-side and pay-side of a D2F sale bind the payout plan version at two different moments of the payment lifecycle - settlement in 20.04.03, authorization in 20.04.04 - and each states its moment normatively and repeatedly.
findings.evidence: 20.04-direct-to-fan-storefront/20.04.03-digital-sales-name-your-price-bundles.md:108 - "The payout plan **version** is bound at **payment settlement**, not at add-to-cart, and the entitlement records that version." Against: 20.04-direct-to-fan-storefront/20.04.04-d2f-revenue-split-payout.md:99 - "Split applied at payment authorization against the plan version live at that instant"; same file line 115 - "Prior sales pay the plan version live at their payment authorization ... Each sale is locked to the split version live at the moment it is authorized - a domain 09 edit mid-checkout does not re-bind an in-flight sale."; line 120 - "Two simultaneous sales each lock to the split version live at their own authorization instant"; line 121 - "the accrual applies the split version that was live when the sale was authorized".
findings.forcedInvention: An implementer must invent which payment-lifecycle instant binds the payout plan version to a sale.
findings.failure_scenario: A drummer's ownership dispute resolves in domain 09 at 14:02, changing a split from 10% to 20%. A fan's card is authorized at 14:00 and the charge settles at 14:05. Binding at authorization pays the drummer 10%; binding at settlement pays 20%. On a catalogue selling continuously either choice is defensible, but the two produce different money for a real payee on the same sale, and 20.04.04's own statement line is specified to name the governing version - so the discrepancy is visible to the payee.

findings.claim: The 20.04 cross-cut file still records bundle partial refunds as the unsolved case with an untracked [PENDING], after 20.04.03 D-06 resolved it by name and the domain-level cross-cut file restates that resolution as settled. The marker has no owner and contradicts a decision that cites it.
findings.evidence: 20.04-direct-to-fan-storefront/20.04-direct-to-fan-storefront-cx.md:40 - "5. **State transition conflict**: **Partial refund is the unsolved case.** `[PENDING - /ideate-discover Step 5 deepening]`. A cancelled pressing means refunding the physical portion while the digital stands - but the fan paid one price for one thing, and apportioning it after the fact is arbitrary." Against: 20.04-direct-to-fan-storefront/20.04.03-digital-sales-name-your-price-bundles.md:159 - "| D-06 | Partial refunds use component notional values captured at listing, scaled to the price paid | Resolves `-cx.md` CX-01 Q5 (see DT-04). Deterministic, auditable, refund never exceeds what was paid. |"; and fanbase-direct-to-fan-cx.md:331 - "Component notional values captured at listing drive deterministic partial-refund apportionment (D-06)."
findings.forcedInvention: None - the rule exists at 20.04.03 D-06; the defect is that the sub-domain cross-cut file asserts the opposite with a marker carrying no owner.
findings.failure_scenario: An implementer specifying bundle refund behaviour opens the sub-domain cross-cut file, which is the canonical place for cross-component interaction rules, reads that apportionment is unsolved and arbitrary, and either blocks the slice or implements a support-decided manual refund - the exact design 20.04.03 DT-04 rejected and replaced with captured notionals.

findings.claim: The 10% rolling reserve is defined in the parameter table as a percentage of each disbursement, but is described everywhere else in the same file as held per sale at accrual. Because the reserve carries a 90-day release window sized to the card chargeback window, the two readings start that clock on different dates.
findings.evidence: 20.04-direct-to-fan-storefront/20.04.04-d2f-revenue-split-payout.md:58 - "| **Rolling reserve** | **10%** of each disbursement held **90 days**, released if no refund/chargeback/dispute touches the originating sale |". Against, in the same file: line 99 - "artist \u00a38.82, producer \u00a32.52, drummer \u00a31.26 - each accrues immediately, each with a 10% reserve held for 90 days"; line 29 (Role Lens) - "Sees per sale where the money went: gross, platform cut, each payee's share, the 10% rolling reserve held"; line 135 (Populated state) - "Per-sale breakdown: gross, platform cut, basis ..., each payee's share, 10% reserve held, disbursement status". Line 114 fixes the window's purpose - "The 90-day reserve window is sized to the typical card chargeback window so most land inside it" - which only holds if the clock starts at the sale.
findings.forcedInvention: An implementer must invent whether the reserve is computed and clocked per sale at accrual or per batch at disbursement.
findings.failure_scenario: A payee accrues 6p per micro-sale and does not cross the GBP 20 disbursement threshold for five months. Under the per-sale reading each sale's reserve has already released before the payout runs, so the disbursement carries no reserve and a late chargeback has nothing to reverse against. Under the per-disbursement reading the 90-day clock starts five months after the transactions it is meant to cover, so it lapses long after the chargeback window closed. Either way the mechanism D-08 relies on to avoid issuing debt demands to collaborators fails, and the file does not say which behaviour to build.

findings.claim: The two files that state the interim keep-on-lapse behaviour define two different sets of surviving items - items the fan opened while entitled, versus items released while the fan was paying - and 20.06.03 presents its version as a restatement of 20.05.02's.
findings.evidence: 20.06-fan-experience-discovery/20.06.03-fan-library-collection.md:120 - "on lapse, per [20.05.02](...) DT-02's leaning, items **released while the fan was paying stay accessible** and future items lock." Against: 20.05-memberships-patronage-campaigns/20.05.02-exclusive-content-vault.md:73 - "until ratified, the safe default is no retroactive removal (matches D-05); **items opened while entitled** stay accessible." The two are not the same set: an item posted in month 3 of a 14-month membership and never opened is inside 20.06.03's set and outside 20.05.02's. 20.05.02 D-05 ("A raised minimum tier does not retroactively remove access") is about access rather than opening and does not disambiguate.
findings.forcedInvention: An implementer must invent whether an unopened item released during the membership survives the lapse.
findings.failure_scenario: A fan is a member for 14 months, during which the artist posts 40 vault items; the fan opens 12. On lapse, an implementer following 20.05.02 locks 28 items; one following 20.06.03 locks none of the 40 and only future posts. The fan-visible outcome differs by 28 items, and 20.06.03's own specified UI - greyed rows reading 'Renew to access' - renders whichever set the implementer chose as if it were the settled policy.

findings.claim: 20.06.02 D-05 makes an alerting SLO a normative requirement and distinguishes it from a retryable queue, but names no target value and no file, decision or open question in the domain routes the value to any owner or stage - unlike every other numeric calibration in this domain, which is explicitly deferred.
findings.evidence: 20.06-fan-experience-discovery/20.06.02-gig-alerts-near-me.md:114 - "| D-05 | Alert dispatch has an SLO, not a queue | A missed alert is not a retryable job - the show happened without them, which is the exact failure the product exists to prevent. |"; the same requirement in the States table at line 82 - "**The fan misses the show.** Not a retryable background job - it is time-critical, unrepeatable, and the single job the product exists to do. Needs an alerting SLO, not a queue." That file's Q-01 through Q-05 cover the mobile surface, third-party listings, location capture, festival aggregation and the radius conflict; none covers the SLO. By contrast 20.01.01 Q-04 explicitly routes the comparable value - "the SLA/backstop after which a persistently unresolved queued observation (D-05) is flagged for manual review" - to `/create-prd-architecture` with a named owner.
findings.forcedInvention: An implementer must invent the dispatch latency target that distinguishes a met alert SLO from a missed one, and there is no owner or stage to escalate to.
findings.failure_scenario: The on-sale fires and the alert fan-out to 4,000 followers takes 90 minutes behind a transient provider slowdown. With no stated target, no monitor alarms and no one is paged; the tickets sell out in 40 minutes and several hundred fans miss the show the feature exists to catch. Nothing in the spec lets a reviewer say the SLO was breached, because no SLO value was ever written or assigned to anyone to write.
